metric.why: Rates rising after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply. Rate data is compiled by commercial research firms listed in the directory below; it is not republished here.
metric.definition: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.

reading.body:
Colocation rental rates are the price signal for data center scarcity, and the direction given here is up after a decade of decline.

The metric is priced per kilowatt per month, not per square foot. That unit is the point: what the market is charging for is delivered power, not building space. A metro where the rate rises is a metro where power and the capacity to deliver it are short relative to demand. The decade of decline beforehand is what makes the reversal informative, because the data treats the turn as the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply.

For AI this is the cost of renting the ground that models run on. Operators that lease rather than build pay this rate directly, and it sets the price against which building their own capacity is judged. When the rate climbs, the market is telling builders that leased capacity is worth more than it cost to provide.

What the data does not contain is any rate, metro, date, or magnitude. It defines the metric and asserts a direction, and attributes the underlying figures to commercial research firms that are not republished here. A reader cannot tell from this how large the increase is, how much it varies between metros, or whether it has continued.
